name: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten / Hybrid)

lead: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten, Methyl-Sten, Ultradrol) is a synthetic oral androgen, the 17-alpha-methylated derivative of stenbolone. Lifters use it seeking muscle gain and a harder physique. It was never introduced for medical use.

It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist, and 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity. Published work is mainly metabolism and doping-detection studies, supplement analyses and a case report; it has not been trialled in people.

paras: It has been sold online as a nutritional supplement or research chemical in oral form.
A case report links a product containing it to cholestatic jaundice. It is prohibited in sport and has no approved medical use.

angle.text: It activates the androgen receptor, the route to faster muscle protein gain and a harder-looking physique, and lifters use it for that. It has never been trialled in people; the published human material is a case report of cholestatic jaundice.

lead: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten, Methyl-Sten, Ultradrol) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methylated derivative of stenbolone. It was never introduced for medical use and has been sold online as a nutritional supplement.[1][2]
Published work consists mainly of metabolism and doping-detection studies, supplement analyses and a case report of cholestatic jaundice.[3][4][5][6]

paras: It is described as a 17-alpha-alkylated androstane with a 2-alpha-methyl group; the 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity and liver burden.[2]

No studies found of methylstenbolone in a clinical trial. A 2014 case report described cholestatic jaundice in a person using a supplement found to contain methylstenbolone and dymethazine.[6] A 2023 analysis examined androgenic steroids in over-the-counter supplements and adverse health effects.[7]

A 2013 study detected it in a supplement and described urinary metabolites; later work identified long-term metabolites for doping control, used human liver microsomes and a chimeric mouse model, and studied metabolism in horses.[3][4][5][8] Methylstenbolone is prohibited in sport.[8]
